title: How Individualism Changed the Way We Read the Bible
excerpt: We did not stop believing the Bible, we quietly rewrote who it was talking to, and the someone it now addresses is me alone.
body:
A man stands in my office and tells me God has a plan for his life. He means his life. Singular. The job, the move, the woman he is unsure about. I believe God is at work in all of it. But I notice what he does not notice, which is that the sentence he reached for to describe the will of God landed entirely inside the borders of one person, and that person is himself. He did not learn that sentence from Scripture. He learned it from the air he breathes.

The question is not whether God cares about individuals. He does, down to the hairs of the head. The question is whether the individual has become the only unit we can see, the lens so close to the eye that we no longer recognize it as a lens. We think we are reading the Bible. We are often reading ourselves into it, and calling the echo revelation.

## The Lens Too Close to the Eye

Let me give the strongest version of the other side, because it is strong. The defender of the personal Bible will say that the gospel really is personal, that Jesus left the ninety nine for the one, that Paul writes I have been crucified with Christ, that conversion is not a committee vote, that every believer stands before God without a mediator but Christ, and that the Reformation itself fought and bled for the conscience of the single soul against the machinery of the institution. All of that is true. I would die on that ground. The recovery of the individual conscience before God is one of the great gifts of the church to the world, and the skeptic who values his own freedom of conscience is living, whether he knows it or not, on borrowed Christian capital.

> We think we are reading the Bible. We are often reading ourselves into it, and calling the echo revelation.

But here is what that argument gets right and then takes too far. It is true that I am saved as a person. It is not true that I am saved as an isolate. The same Paul who says I have been crucified with Christ spends most of his ink writing to churches, in the plural, about a body with many members, and almost every you that English readers hear as singular is in the Greek a you that means all of you together. We read a letter written to a congregation as if it were a note left on my pillow.

## What the Reformation Gave and Where We Took It Too Far

Carry one text through this. When Jeremiah delivers the most quoted promise in the American devotional, For I know the plans I have for you, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope (Jeremiah 29:11 ESV), he is not whispering to a discouraged individual about a career change. He is writing a letter to a nation in exile in Babylon, a deported people, telling them to build houses, plant gardens, marry, and seek the welfare of the very city that conquered them, because their God has not abandoned the community even in captivity. The you is a people. The plan is corporate, generational, costly, and seventy years long. We took a word spoken over a traumatized nation and shrank it to fit a coffee mug.

## The Letter Written to a Nation

How did this happen. Trace it. Robert Bellah and his colleagues, studying American life in the early 1980s, named the thing precisely. They called it expressive individualism, the conviction that each person has a unique core of feeling and intuition that must be unfolded if individuality is to be realized, and they showed how even the most religious Americans had absorbed it so deeply that they described their faith in the language of personal preference (Bellah 1985). One woman in their study named her own religion after herself. Sheilaism. Charles Taylor traced the longer arc, the slow construction across five centuries of what he calls the buffered self, the modern interior shielded from the world, sealed off, the meaning of a life generated from inside rather than received from outside (Taylor 2007). The porous self of the ancient world, open to God and neighbor and the dead, became the buffered self of the mall, open mainly to its own desires.

The church did not resist this. The church baptized it. By the time American revivalism had run its course through the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, the altar call had made the decision of the individual the hinge of everything, which is half a glory and half a wound. The glory is that no one is saved by belonging to a crowd. The wound is that we began to imagine the crowd did not matter at all, that a Christian is a sovereign consumer of religious goods who attends a church the way he subscribes to a service, retaining at all times the right to cancel.

## How the Buffered Self Was Built

Now watch the reversal, because Scripture refuses our flattery. The most individual moment in the Bible, a man alone in a garden at night, sweating blood, is the moment Jesus is least alone in purpose, because he is there for a body he is about to gather out of the whole earth. He prays not for himself but for them, and not only for these, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that they may all be one (John 17:20 ESV). The cross is the most personal act in history and the least private. He died, one man, for a people. The pronoun is singular at the nail and plural at the empty tomb.

> We took a word spoken over a traumatized nation and shrank it to fit a coffee mug.

This is where law has to come before grace, and the law is this. If I read the Bible as a private message to me, I will use it. I will mine it for the verses that serve my plans and skip the ones that bind me to people I did not choose. I will treat the church as a vendor and my neighbor as scenery. And I will do all of this with a Bible open on my lap, sincerely, never once suspecting that I have made the living God into an accessory to a life I was going to live anyway. That is not a small sin. That is the slow theft of the whole counsel of God, one comforting verse at a time. I have done it. I do it on the mornings I am tired and want the text to console me rather than command me.

## The Pronoun Singular at the Nail, Plural at the Tomb

The grace is that the God of the letter to Babylon does not abandon the captives, even the captives of our own age, even the ones whose captivity is so comfortable they call it freedom. He still writes to a people. He is still building a house with many rooms and many members, and he means to put me in it next to someone I would not have picked, and call that salvation.

So read the next verse you love and ask the question first. Who is the you. If the answer turns out to be all of you together, and it almost always does, then the verse was never the private property you thought it was. It was a word to a people, and you were being invited to stop being an audience of one.

> The cross is the most personal act in history and the least private.

We made the Bible smaller to make ourselves larger. The book will not stay that size.

### Works Cited

Bellah, Robert N., Richard Madsen, William M. Sullivan, Ann Swidler, and Steven M. Tipton. Habits of the Heart: Individualism and Commitment in American Life. Berkeley: University of California Press, 1985.

Taylor, Charles. A Secular Age. Cambridge, MA: Belknap Press of Harvard University Press, 2007.

The Holy Bible. English Standard Version. Wheaton: Crossway, 2001.

title: Consumerism Is a Spiritual Formation
excerpt: The mall is not neutral, it is a cathedral, and we have been worshiping in it longer than we have been worshiping anywhere else.
body:
My sons can tell the difference between two phones I cannot see a difference between. They were not taught this in any class. No one sat them down. They absorbed it the way I absorbed my father's absence, which is to say through the body, through repetition, through a thousand small mornings that added up to a shape before anyone named the shape. They have been formed. The question that should keep a pastor awake is not whether they have been formed but by what, and toward what end.

We assume that what makes us who we are is what we believe. State the doctrine, win the mind, and the life follows. This is the great quiet error of the modern church, and I held it for years. We built ministries on the premise that the human being is fundamentally a thinker, a brain on a stick, and that if we could only get the right information into the head the body would fall in line. So we lectured. We informed. And we watched people who could pass a theology exam live indistinguishably from their unbelieving neighbors, and we blamed their willpower, when the problem was never the head.

## The Brain on a Stick

Here is the strongest case for the way we have done it, and it deserves respect. Truth matters. Doctrine is not optional. The mind is not nothing, and a faith that cannot say what it believes is a feeling waiting to evaporate. The long Christian tradition of catechism, of teaching the faith as content, saved generations from sentimentality and heresy alike. A church that stops caring whether things are true has already begun to die. I will not give an inch on that. The skeptic who prizes evidence and clear thinking is closer to the kingdom than the believer who prizes a warm vague glow.

> You are not primarily what you think. You are what you love, and you do not choose your loves the way you choose your beliefs.

But here is where that case runs out. You are not primarily what you think. You are what you love, and you do not choose your loves the way you choose your beliefs. James K. A. Smith put it as sharply as anyone has in a generation. He argues that human beings are desiring creatures before we are thinking creatures, that we are shaped most deeply not by ideas we consider but by practices we repeat, by what he calls cultural liturgies, the rituals that aim our love at something before our mind ever weighs in (Smith 2009). And the most powerful liturgy in the modern world is not held in a church. It is held in a mall, and now it is held in your hand.

## You Are What You Love

Walk through what the mall does, because Smith is right that it is a temple and we should say so plainly. It has a clean and beautiful interior set apart from the street. It has icons in the windows, images of the redeemed life, bodies made perfect, the promise of belonging. It has an order of service. You enter, you wander, you are met by ministers who help you find your size, you make your sacrifice at the register, and you leave carrying a small sacrament in a bag, briefly fuller, soon empty, certain to return. No one believes a doctrine here. Everyone is being formed here. The mall does not care what you think about the mall. It only needs you to keep coming, and you do.

## The Mall Is a Temple

Carry one text. Jesus does not say where your treasure is, there your thinking will be correct. He says, For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also (Matthew 6:21 ESV). Notice the order. He does not say fix your heart and your spending will follow. He says follow the money and you will find the heart, because the heart goes where the treasure has already gone. Spending is not the symptom. Spending is the formation. Every purchase is a small act of worship that trains the desires a little more, and after ten thousand of them you are a certain kind of person, and you never decided to be.

## The Manufacture of Wanting

Trace the history, because this captivity has a date. The American economy of the early twentieth century faced a crisis the founders of advertising named openly. Production had outrun need. The factories could make more than people wanted. The solution, pioneered by men like Edward Bernays in the 1920s, was to manufacture wants, to attach products to desires that had nothing to do with the product. Bernays famously staged a group of women lighting cigarettes in a public parade, an image his circle framed as torches of freedom, and the method he helped pioneer taught a generation of admakers to bind a product to status or identity rather than to mere use. The point, in his hands and theirs, was to sell the cigarette as emancipation and, later, the car as a self, to graft the product onto a hunger it could never actually satisfy. Jacques Ellul saw the deeper machinery. He argued that modern technique and the propaganda that serves it do not merely persuade us of things, they integrate us into a system, forming the individual to fit the apparatus, so that the person comes to want exactly what the system needs him to want and calls it his own free choice (Ellul 1964). The genius of consumer formation is that it never feels like formation. It feels like me being myself. That is what makes it a liturgy and not an argument.

> The genius of consumer formation is that it never feels like formation. It feels like me being myself.

Now the reversal. We think the danger of consumerism is that it makes us want bad things. The deeper danger is what it does to wanting itself. It trains us to be people who are constituted by acquisition, who resolve every ache by purchasing, who cannot sit in an unsatisfied moment for ninety seconds without reaching for the phone to buy our way out of it. It does not corrupt our desires so much as it corrupts our capacity to desire God, who cannot be acquired, who will not fit in the bag, who asks not to be consumed but to be loved. A people trained for sixty years to fill every emptiness will not know what to do with a God who sometimes leaves the emptiness in order to fill it himself.

> I have preached against the mall on Sunday and shopped my way through Monday's anxiety, and the gap between those two days is the size of my actual discipleship.

Law before grace, and the law is heavy. I am formed by this. I do not stand above it as a diagnostician. I reach for my phone in the silence. I have measured my worth by what I could afford and felt the lift of a purchase and called that lift joy. I have preached against the mall on Sunday and shopped my way through Monday's anxiety, and the gap between those two days is the size of my actual discipleship. The honest word is that the liturgies of the market have catechized me more hours than the church ever has, and it is not close.

## Counter Formation at the Table

The grace is that formation answers formation. If we are shaped by repeated practice and not by single decisions, then the worn old disciplines of the church are not quaint, they are counter formation, deliberate liturgies aimed at retraining a heart the market has trained against itself. The Lord's table is the anti mall, a meal you cannot buy, a sacrifice already made, a belonging you did not shop for. The Sabbath is a refusal to produce or to purchase for one day in seven, a weekly act of treason against an economy that needs you restless. These are not tips. They are the slow reconstruction of a person, and like all formation they work only by repetition, only by years, only by showing up to the table on the mornings you would rather be at the store.

We became what we bought while we were busy guarding what we believed.

The heart went where the treasure went. It always does.

### Works Cited

Smith, James K. A. Desiring the Kingdom: Worship, Worldview, and Cultural Formation. Grand Rapids: Baker Academic, 2009.

Ellul, Jacques. The Technological Society. Translated by John Wilkinson. New York: Vintage Books, 1964.

The Holy Bible. English Standard Version. Wheaton: Crossway, 2001.

title: The Church Held Captive to the Culture War
excerpt: We were promised the culture war would defend the faith, and instead it quietly rewrote the faith to fit the war.
body:
A man left my church a few years ago not over a doctrine but over a vote. He could not understand how I could shepherd people who voted the other way. He said it as a matter of faithfulness, and he meant it. What unsettled me was not that he was political. We are all political, and the gospel has public weight or it has none. What unsettled me was that he could no longer locate his deepest loyalty. When I asked him gently what he believed about the cross, he answered me with a position on a policy. The grammar had shifted underneath him, and he had not noticed, and I am not sure I would have noticed in his place.

The real question is not whether Christians should care about justice and law and the shape of the common life. We must. The question is what happens to a church when the framework through which it sees everything is no longer the kingdom of God but the war between two tribes, when the categories that organize the Christian mind are imported wholesale from a politics that was not built to carry the weight of the soul.

## The Prophet and the Captive

Here is the strongest defense of Christian engagement in the culture war, and it is not weak. The faith makes claims about reality. It says the unborn child is a person, that marriage has a given shape, that there is such a thing as truth, that the powerful will answer for the vulnerable. These are not private opinions to be kept behind the church door. They are public truths, and a church that retreats into a spiritual interior while the world burns has abandoned the prophets, who stood in the gates of the city and named the sins of the nation by name. The believer who fights for the weak in the public square is doing something the Bible commands. To call that captivity would be a slander. I hold these convictions. I have not softened them.

> You are a chaplain to a faction, and the faction owns you.

But here is what that defense cannot account for. There is a difference between the church speaking prophetically to the powers and the church being captured by one of the powers. The prophet stands outside the kingdoms and judges them all by a higher throne. The captive stands inside one kingdom and judges the other in its terms, and calls his captivity courage. The test is simple and brutal. When your political tribe does the very thing you condemned in the other tribe, do you say so. If the answer is no, if the sin becomes acceptable the moment your side commits it, then you are not a prophet. You are a chaplain to a faction, and the faction owns you.

## The Oldest Temptation on the Mountain

Carry one text, the oldest temptation, told as a true story. The devil took him to a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. And he said to him, All these I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me (Matthew 4:8 ESV). Read it slowly. The offer was the kingdoms. The offer was real power, real influence, the levers of the nations placed in the hand of the Son of God, and it would have skipped the cross entirely. The price was a single act of worship redirected. Not the abandonment of the kingdoms. The reordering of worship to obtain them. That is the precise shape of the church's captivity. We are not offered evil. We are offered influence, and asked only to bow slightly, to make the cause the thing and the cross the instrument, and we tell ourselves we are still worshiping God while we do it.

## The Hollowing of the Theological Center

Trace the history, because this is older and more bipartisan than we admit. In the early 1980s a coalition formed that fused a wing of the American church to a political movement with a discipline neither had known before. It delivered real victories and a real cost, and the cost was that a generation of believers learned to read their Bibles through a partisan lens so total that the parties began to function as denominations. David Wells, watching the church across these decades, named the underlying disease before the politics ever crystallized. He argued that the evangelical church had already hollowed out its theology, had traded the weight of truth for the techniques of relevance and success, so that when the culture war came it found a church with no theological center strong enough to resist being annexed by something with a center of its own (Wells 1993). A church that had stopped being formed by its doctrine was available to be formed by its politics, and it was, and so was the church on the other side, the progressive congregation that discovered its entire moral vocabulary had quietly been issued by the latest social movement, with the cross retained as decoration.

Neil Postman saw the mechanism that made all of this possible and worse. He argued that the move of public life onto the screen does not merely change what we know, it changes the form of knowing itself, dissolving argument into image and conviction into entertainment, so that a culture organized around the television and now the feed comes to experience even its most serious commitments as a kind of show (Postman 1985). The culture war is not primarily a war of ideas. It is a war of feelings staged for an audience, and the church walked onto that stage carrying the gospel and started performing it for applause, and forgot it was holding something that was meant to be died for, not posted.

## Conscripted From the Inside

> We came to save the faith and we let the faith be conscripted, and the proof is that for many of us it now costs more to break with our political side than to break with our Lord.

Now the reversal, and it cuts. We entered the culture war to defend the faith. The war did not destroy the faith from outside. It rewrote it from inside. It taught us to feel our deepest belonging with our tribe and only our nominal belonging with the brother across the aisle who shares our baptism. It made the enemy a category of people rather than the principalities and powers Paul actually names. We came to save the faith and we let the faith be conscripted, and the proof is that for many of us it now costs more to break with our political side than to break with our Lord. We would lose more friends. That sentence should stop us cold.

> I have measured a brother by his vote before I measured him by his cross.

Law before grace, and I am inside the law. I have felt the warm pull of the applause line, the sermon that lands because it confirms what my people already wanted to hate. I have measured a brother by his vote before I measured him by his cross. I have been quieter about the sins of my own side because quiet was cheaper, and I have called that prudence when it was cowardice. The captivity does not happen to other pastors in other states. It happens at my desk, on the weeks I want my people to love me more than I want them to be free.

## The One Who Refused the Kingdoms

The grace runs straight through the temptation in the wilderness, because the one being offered the kingdoms refused them, and went and got them another way, by the cross, by dying, by rising, by a throne no election confers and no defeat removes. He owns the kingdoms now, all of them, the ones my tribe runs and the ones the other tribe runs, and he holds them so lightly and so surely that he can ask me to love my political enemy without fear, because the outcome was never riding on my faction. The kingdom does not need my captivity to advance. It only needs my allegiance, and allegiance has only ever had room for one throne.

The war promised to make us strong. It made us loud, and then it made us its own.

Not a prophet to the nation. A chaplain to a faction. We can still tell the difference, if we are willing to fail the tribe's test on purpose.

### Works Cited

Wells, David F. No Place for Truth: Or Whatever Happened to Evangelical Theology. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 1993.

Postman, Neil. Amusing Ourselves to Death: Public Discourse in the Age of Show Business. New York: Viking, 1985.

The Holy Bible. English Standard Version. Wheaton: Crossway, 2001.

title: Outrage Is Not a Spiritual Gift
excerpt: We mistook the heat of our anger for the fire of the Spirit, and the machine that sells our attention was happy to let us believe it.
body:
I caught myself last week reaching for my phone before I had finished the prayer. Not after. During. There was a thing happening online, an outrage cycling through the people I follow, and my body wanted to be in it the way a younger man wants to be in a fight. I noticed the hunger and it frightened me, because it was not a hunger for righteousness. It was a hunger for the feeling of righteousness, which is a different and more dangerous thing, and I had been trained to crave it by an instrument I carry in my pocket and call a tool.

The question underneath the noise is whether our public anger is the holy thing we tell ourselves it is. We call it standing for truth. We quote the prophets. We remember that Jesus made a whip and cleared the temple, and we use that one afternoon to justify a permanent disposition of fury at strangers. The question is whether the anger forming us is the anger of God or the anger of the algorithm, and whether we have lost the ability to tell them apart.

## The Hunger for the Feeling of Righteousness

Give the strongest case for the anger, because there is one. Some things ought to make us furious. A world without holy anger is a world that has made peace with cruelty. The prophets burned. Jesus wept over a city and overturned tables in a temple. The abolitionist who was not enraged by the slave market had a defective conscience, not a mature one. Anger at genuine evil is not a sin, it is a sign of life, the proof that you still love something enough to be wounded when it is violated. A faith that produces only mild men who are upset by nothing is not Christianity, it is sedation. I will defend righteous anger. Scripture commands it.

## A Clock on the Anger

> It treats holy anger the way you treat a controlled burn, useful, necessary, and one gust of wind from destroying the whole field.

But here is where the case collapses under its own weight. The Bible never treats anger as a reliable indicator of righteousness. It treats it as a fire that must be watched every moment it burns. Be angry and do not sin, Paul writes, and then immediately, do not let the sun go down on your anger, and give no opportunity to the devil (Ephesians 4:26 ESV). Read what that assumes. It assumes anger, even permitted anger, even righteous anger, is precisely the doorway through which the enemy enters, that it has a shelf life of hours, that it spoils by nightfall and becomes something the devil can use. The text does not celebrate the anger. It puts a clock on it. It treats holy anger the way you treat a controlled burn, useful, necessary, and one gust of wind from destroying the whole field.

## Farmed for Rage

> We did not stumble into a culture of rage. We were farmed for it.

Now here is the part we will not want to hear. The machine that delivers our anger to us was engineered, deliberately, to make sure the sun never goes down on it. Trace the history. In 2009 the major platforms gave us the instruments of measurement, the Facebook like button in February and the Twitter retweet button that November, with the frictionless share spreading across the web in the years on either side, small buttons that turned communication into a tally. Engineers learned quickly what kept people on the screen, and it was not joy and it was not peace. It was moral emotion, and the most engaging moral emotion is outrage at an outgroup. The systems were then tuned, by optimization more than by malice, to surface exactly the content that made us angriest at people not like us, because angry people scroll, angry people share, and angry people return. Jonathan Haidt has assembled the data with care, showing that the years following this redesign tracked with a sharp rise in adolescent anxiety, depression, and self harm beginning around 2012, especially among girls, a generation rewired by the very engines of moral outrage and social comparison they were handed before they could drive (Haidt 2024). We did not stumble into a culture of rage. We were farmed for it.

Marshall McLuhan said the thing decades before the engineers proved him right. The medium is the message. The form of a technology shapes us more than any content we pour through it, and we are constitutionally blind to the form because we are mesmerized by the content (McLuhan 1964). We argue about what to post. The medium has already decided what we are becoming by posting, and what we are becoming is people for whom the resting state of the soul is a low grade fury looking for an object.

## The Machine Does Not Care Which Side

Carry the reversal here. We believe we are using the outrage to fight evil. The outrage is using us to feed the machine, and the machine does not care which side we are on. It profits identically from the rage of the right and the rage of the left. It will hand the progressive his daily villain and the conservative hers, and bill them both, and call it engagement. The most sobering fact about Christian outrage online is that it is indistinguishable in form from every other outrage, runs on the same fuel, serves the same masters, and produces the same fruit, which Paul lists plainly as enmity, strife, fits of anger, rivalries, dissensions, divisions, the works of the flesh wearing the costume of conviction.

Law before grace, and I am the chief defendant. I have felt the rush of the righteous post and refreshed the screen to count who agreed. I have been angrier at a stranger on the internet than at my own sin, which is the exact inversion of the gospel order. I have let the sun go down on it, and the next sun, and called the residue zeal. I have modeled this for my five sons, who watch their father reach for the glowing rectangle in the silence, and learn from the reaching what their father actually treasures. The outrage was never a spiritual gift. It was a work of the flesh I had dressed in Scripture so I would not have to repent of it.

## The Fruit the Algorithm Cannot Sell

The grace is that the Spirit produces something the algorithm cannot manufacture and cannot sell. Against the works of the flesh Paul sets the fruit of the Spirit, and it begins with love and ends with self control, and in the middle, impossibly, it lists peace and patience and gentleness, the precise traits the machine is built to burn out of us (Galatians 5:22 ESV). The Spirit grows slowly and the algorithm rewards instantly, and a person can tell which one is forming him by asking what he is becoming. More peaceful or more reactive. More patient or more triggered. Gentler with his children or quicker to the phone. The fruit does not lie, and it does not trend.

> We thought our anger proved we still cared. It proved we had been captured.

We thought our anger proved we still cared. It proved we had been captured.

Let the sun go down on it. That is not weakness. That is the first free act in a long captivity.

### Works Cited

Haidt, Jonathan. The Anxious Generation: How the Great Rewiring of Childhood Is Causing an Epidemic of Mental Illness. New York: Penguin Press, 2024.

McLuhan, Marshall. Understanding Media: The Extensions of Man. New York: McGraw-Hill, 1964.

The Holy Bible. English Standard Version. Wheaton: Crossway, 2001.

title: Formed by Screens: Technology and the Soul
excerpt: The screen does not only fill our time, it slowly remakes the kind of soul we have time for.
body:
My youngest can find a video faster than I can find my keys. He is not corrupt. He is a boy with a boy's open face, and he loves his mother and asks me hard questions about God at bedtime. But I have watched something happen to his attention over a season, a fraying, a difficulty in staying with one slow thing, and I cannot honestly blame him, because I have watched the same fraying happen to me. I sit down to read Scripture and my hand reaches for the phone before my mind has settled, and the reaching is so automatic that it has stopped feeling like a choice. Something is forming us both, and it is not the Word.

The question is not whether technology is good or evil. That question is too small and too old, and it always ends in a shrug about how anything can be used well or badly. The real question is sharper. What kind of person does a given technology make of you simply by being used as it was designed to be used. Not abused. Used. Because every tool carries inside it a hidden curriculum, a way of forming the one who holds it, and the screen has a curriculum, and we have all enrolled, and most of us never read the syllabus.

## The Hidden Curriculum of the Tool

Give the strongest case for the screen, and give it honestly. These devices are astonishing gifts. I can carry the whole of Scripture, the Fathers, the Reformers, and a thousand sermons in one hand. A grandmother sees her grandchild's face across an ocean. A man in a remote village hears the gospel he could never have reached in print. The pandemic years would have been unbearable without the screen that kept the lonely connected to the living. To call all of this captivity would be ungrateful and untrue, the grumbling of a man who wishes for a past that was never as holy as he remembers. Technology is a good gift of a creative God to creative creatures. I use it to write the words you are reading. I will not pretend otherwise.

> It abolishes the capacity for silence, and silence is where the soul learns to hear.

But here is what the grateful case keeps stepping around. A tool is not only what it does for you. It is what it does to you while you use it, and these two are often opposites. Charles Taylor described the modern self as buffered, sealed off from a world that once pressed in on it from every side, and the screen is the final architecture of that buffering, the wall made portable and pleasant (Taylor 2007). It promises to connect us and it insulates us. It puts a pane of glass between me and the man across the table, between me and the slow boredom out of which prayer is born, between me and my own unmanaged thoughts, which are exactly the thoughts in which God has always done his quietest work. The screen does not merely occupy the silence. It abolishes the capacity for silence, and silence is where the soul learns to hear.

## The God Who Speaks in a Whisper

Carry one text, and let it be strange enough to wake us. After the wind and the earthquake and the fire, none of which held the Lord, there came a low whisper. And when Elijah heard it, he wrapped his face in his cloak and went out (1 Kings 19:12 ESV). God was not in the spectacle. He was in the whisper, the sound that requires a quiet so deep that a man would have to have built his whole life around the practice of listening to hear it at all. Now ask the honest question. Could the version of me that checks the phone in the silence of his own prayers hear a whisper. The screen is a technology of the wind and the earthquake and the fire, endless spectacle, endless noise, and a God who speaks in a whisper is a God we have engineered ourselves to miss.

## Technique Made Intimate

Trace the history, because formation by tools is not new, only newly total. Jacques Ellul argued in the middle of the last century that the deepest danger of modern life is not any single machine but technique itself, the relentless drive toward efficiency that subordinates every human end to the question of what works, until the person is reshaped to serve the apparatus rather than the apparatus the person (Ellul 1964). The screen is technique made intimate. Neil Postman, building on this, warned that the move from the printed word to the image does not just change our entertainment, it changes the structure of our thought, training us for fragments and against arguments, for stimulation and against contemplation, until a whole civilization loses the patience that sustained things like reading a long book or sitting with a hard truth or praying without a phone in reach (Postman 1985). They saw the river's direction before most of us felt the current. We are now far downstream.

## Formed by Ten Thousand Small Acts

Here is the reversal, and it is the one that matters most. We believe we are using these devices to save time, and we are, and then we have no idea what the saved time was for, so we give it back to the same devices, and we are formed not by the content we consume but by the ten thousand small acts of consuming, the reach, the scroll, the flick, the refresh, repeated until they are no longer things we do but the shape of who we are. The danger was never that the screen would make us believe something false. The danger is that it would make us into a certain kind of soul, restless, distractible, incapable of the long slow attention that love and prayer and presence require, and that it would do this so gently we would mistake the new self for the only self we ever had.

> I have been bodily present with my sons and mentally somewhere in a feed, and they know the difference even when I pretend they do not, because children read presence the way the rest of us read words.

Law before grace, and the law has my name on it. I have prayed with one ear on the notification. I have been bodily present with my sons and mentally somewhere in a feed, and they know the difference even when I pretend they do not, because children read presence the way the rest of us read words. I have told my congregation that God speaks in the whisper and then lived a life arranged so that no whisper could ever reach me. I am not the doctor here. I am the patient, and the diagnosis is the same one I would write for the man in my office who cannot sit still long enough to be loved by God.

## Repentance With a Body

The grace is that we are formed creatures, which means we can be re formed, and the church has known the medicine for two thousand years. The old disciplines of silence and solitude and fasting are not nostalgia. They are deliberate counter formation, structured acts of refusing the wind and the earthquake and the fire so that the whisper has a chance to land. To put the phone in another room and sit in the unbearable quiet until it stops being unbearable is not a productivity hack. It is repentance with a body, the slow undoing of a formation we did not choose, the clearing of enough silence that a God who has been whispering the whole time can finally be heard saying what he said to Elijah, which was not condemnation but a question, gentle and terrible. What are you doing here.

> The screen did not steal our time. It quietly stole the kind of soul that has time for God.

The screen did not steal our time. It quietly stole the kind of soul that has time for God.

Not a tool we are using. A liturgy that is using us. We can still walk out into the silence, wrap our faces, and listen.
